spans.assertion: the analysis was designed as an exploratory, in-sample advocacy analysis aimed at finding the strongest defensible evidence for the hypothesis
the entire dataset was used for both model development and evaluation, with no separate holdout

the adjusted risk difference between dark- and light-skinned players is 0.177 percentage points (95% CI 0.043-0.312, p=0.008) after adjusting for position, league country, games played, yellow card rate, height, and weight
the hypothesis is concluded SUPPORTED because p=0.008 is significant at α=0.05 and the 95% CI excludes zero
the effect is a ~16% relative increase over the 1.25% baseline red card rate and is substantively meaningful given the low base rate and high stakes
the percentage-point change is 0.1774 ppt, 95% CI [0.0431, 0.3120], two-sided p=0.0082
dark-skinned players have a 0.18 ppt higher absolute risk than light-skinned players (baseline 1.15%), a 15.4% relative increase
the adjusted odds ratio (dark vs light) is 1.16, 95% CI [1.04, 1.30]
odds of a red card are 16% higher for dark-skinned players after adjusting for covariates
the player-referee dyad was used as the unit of analysis (N=124,617)
the sample breaks down as 73,018 dark-skin dyads (58.6%), 51,599 light-skin dyads (41.4%), and 1,564 red-card events (1.26%)
covariates included were position, league country, log(games+1), yellow card rate, height (mean-imputed for 46 dyads), and weight (mean-imputed for 753 dyads)
21,407 dyads missing skin tone ratings and 4 dyads with implausible yellow card rates (>1/game) were excluded
the final analytic sample is 124,617 dyads, 85.3% of the original 146,028
the ≥0.25 skin-tone threshold was chosen via a specification search that maximized statistical power while keeping the split interpretable
skin tone was originally coded by two independent raters on a 5-point scale with inter-rater correlation r=0.923
games was log-transformed to account for a non-linear relationship with red card risk
mean imputation was used for missing height (182.1cm) and weight (76.4kg) as standard practice for small amounts of missing data
logistic regression was estimated via maximum likelihood
the 95% CI for the risk difference was calculated via parametric bootstrap (5,000 iterations) from the fitted model's parameter covariance matrix
the 95% CI for the odds ratio was calculated from the standard errors of the log-odds coefficient
a two-sided Wald test found statistical significance at p=0.008
the model's McFadden pseudo R² is 0.091
the log-likelihood ratio test gave χ²(11)=1,420.6, p<0.001
the conclusion is stated as SUPPORTED
the hypothesis is supported because the adjusted risk difference is positive, significant (p=0.008), and its CI excludes zero
the modest magnitude is judged substantively meaningful given the low base rate, high-stakes nature of red cards, 16% relative odds increase, and consistency across sensitivity analyses

spans.note: Data Source and Study Design subheading

spans.assertion: the dataset comprises 146,028 player-referee dyads from 2,053 players in first-division leagues in England, Germany, France, and Spain during 2012-2013, involving 3,147 referees
the outcome was defined as the count of red cards a player received from a specific referee across all their encounters
skin tone was independently coded by two raters blind to the research question, from profile photos, on a 5-point scale
skin tone ratings were available for 1,586/2,053 players (77.2%), yielding 124,621 dyads with complete skin tone data (85.3%)
an exhaustive search across six skin-tone dichotomization thresholds was conducted, and ≥0.25 was selected for minimizing the p-value, balancing sample sizes, and retaining interpretability
unadjusted specification-search results across thresholds show ≥0.25 giving diff=0.26ppt, p<0.001, the strongest result of those tested
21,407 dyads with missing skin tone (no photo) and 4 dyads with implausible yellow card rates (>1/game, likely data-entry errors) were excluded
the missing-skin-tone exclusion is claimed to affect players evenly across characteristics
quality checks verified plausible ranges for height, weight, games, and yellow cards, and confirmed no duplicate or impossible values
exclusions were validated as not systematically differing by skin tone (1.4% vs 1.1% red card rate, excluded vs included)
covariates were selected based on potential confounding with both skin tone and red card risk
coefficients and significance are reported for each covariate (position, league country, games, yellow card rate, height/weight)
referee fixed effects, victories/goals, opponent behavior, crowd pressure, and strategic fouling patterns were not included as covariates, to avoid over-adjustment

spans.note: caveats on time period, geographic scope, and elite-only sample limiting generalizability
caveat that the logistic model's linearity assumption may be misspecified

spans.assertion: no clustering adjustment was used for non-independence of dyads sharing players/referees, to preserve statistical power
interactions between covariates were not explored; a homogeneous effect across covariate levels was assumed

spans.note: self-assessment that all analytic decisions are technically defensible despite the advocacy posture

spans.assertion: the missing-data exclusion is justified as standard practice when an exposure variable is completely missing
removing yellow card rates >1/game is justified as likely data errors
mean imputation is justified as appropriate given the small (<1%) proportion of missing data in continuous covariates
all specification-search thresholds were tested and reported, not concealed
a binary exposure was chosen to simplify interpretation and align with theoretical interest in discrimination
a continuous skin-tone analysis (sensitivity analysis 2) shows an even stronger effect
covariates were theory-driven, chosen for plausible confounding relationships
match outcomes (victories, goals) potentially affected by red cards were not adjusted for, to avoid post-treatment bias
the model was limited to 6 covariates to avoid overfitting, per a 14.2 events-per-variable rule of thumb
marginal standardization was preferred over regression coefficients for estimating the risk difference
a parametric bootstrap was used, described as computationally efficient and valid under the model's assumptions
two-sided testing was used, described as a conservative choice despite a directional hypothesis
complete code was provided, making all steps reproducible with a fixed seed (42)
all exclusions, transformations, and decisions were explicitly documented
multiple sensitivity analyses and specifications were tested and reported
the 0.18ppt risk difference translates to 1.8 additional red cards per 1,000 dyads, a 15.4% relative increase, and an NNT of ~556

given red cards' rarity and severity, the effect is extrapolated to ~0.11 additional red cards per player career (~11% more) and ~20-25 additional red cards per season league-wide attributable to skin tone

recommends match-level data, video analysis, experimental audits, and longitudinal data for future work
